name: Naiad
lede: Naiad is a soft, light green from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, named for the water nymphs of Greek myth.

sections.title: A water nymph
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* (1930) lists Naiad at plate 27, position B 7, with 1920 as its earliest use, and the NBS Circular 553 of 1955 cites it [1]. The nearest ISCC-NBS category is light green, 4.0 units away [1]. A naiad is a nymph of springs and streams, and the choice of name suggests water-green, though the dictionary does not say why it was chosen [1][2].

The idea is old. Pastoureau quotes a classical passage on dyed dresses that calls a water-colored green the dress of the naiads, which shows the association is no twentieth-century invention [3]. Its neighbors are [[sage]], [[sea-green]] and [[light-green]] [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Naiad appears in 36 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 0.15%, as photographed [5]. It peaks in paintings of the 1900s, in 6 of 1,674 (0.4%), 3.7 times the rate expected from the same museums [5]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light [5]. The earliest match is a painting by Georg Gsell of 1729, 191 years before the name's earliest record, so it is a look-alike hue and not evidence of a dye [5]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [5].
